idiom_name: record UserId(UUID value) with a compact constructor
implementation_notes: Since Java 16 the wrapper collapses into a record: the canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString are generated, and the record is a value-based class by contract. Put validation in the compact constructor so the record itself is the single construction point, and add a static parse for raw input; the missing setters are exactly the immutability the pattern wants. Records still carry reference identity and boxing, so the guarantee is a compile-time one - which is where the pattern's value lives anyway.
pitfalls: Records are not value classes in the JVM: the component is a nullable reference unless the compact constructor rejects null, and a record can still be compared with identity (==) by mistake.

Serialization shape changes: Jackson serializes a record as an object with the component as a property (and older versions need parameter names or @JsonCreator), so the wrapper alters the JSON contract.
Type erasure means List<UserId> and List<UUID> are the same at runtime, and reflection-based frameworks may need explicit converters or constructors.

variants.name: hand-written final value class
variants.idiom_name: final class + private constructor + static factory + equals/hashCode
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-record baseline (Java 8/11): a final class with a private final field, a private constructor guarded by a static factory, and equals/hashCode/toString written once. It is the classic form the pattern was borrowed from in OO languages and still the only option where the JDK floor forbids records; write it once per id type, or centralise it (abstract base class, annotation processor) as soon as the number of wrappers grows.
pitfalls: Forgetting hashCode (or writing equals with getClass in one type and instanceof in another) breaks HashMap/Set lookups - the classic failure of the hand-written form.
A public constructor or a getter that returns a mutable member gradually turns the value class back into a data holder; keep it final and immutable.
Every wrapper repeats the same boilerplate: without a code generator or base class the codebase drifts into inconsistent equality semantics.

variants.name: Lombok @Value generated value class
variants.implementation_notes: Annotation processing writes the immutable class: @Value makes fields private final, adds getters, equals, hashCode and toString and makes the class final - the same shape as the hand-written wrapper, generated. Use it on Java 8+ codebases that already depend on Lombok and cannot move to records; prefer the record once the JDK floor allows it, because the value semantics then belong to the language and not to a processor.
pitfalls: @Value does not implement Comparable, so ordering has to be declared separately - and silently different orderings make sorted collections behave per type.
Generated code is invisible until annotation processing runs: in an IDE or build with the processor disabled, the class looks broken and the error messages point at unrelated code.
